text:
The residency did not have a beach, and I want to be clear about that, because the absence of one was the whole reason the beach trip existed. The colony was a former farm school set in the hills of southern New Hampshire, all red barns and drafty studios, and the nearest ocean was an hour and a half to the east, which for people whose entire lives were conducted in six-week increments of borrowed rooms and temporary mailing addresses was a journey of the same scale as crossing a country.

We had eight weeks there, Toby and I, though our weeks did not quite overlap the way they had been promised. I arrived in the first week and left in the last. He arrived at the potluck in week two, where we met over a dispute concerning a bread knife that both of us claimed to have borrowed from the kitchen and both of us had failed to return. He was a marine biologist, studying the small communities that live between tides, and he had the look of a man who had grown up inland and had decided, somewhere in graduate school, that the ocean was not scenery but a colleague.

I should tell you what we were, without the romance of it. Two people on contracts. My work involved bodies in temporary rooms, which is a description that is accurate and also somehow insulting to my profession. His involved mud flats and tide tables and a clipboard he carried everywhere like a small, damp shield. Neither of us had said the word after, not once in six weeks, because we were both competent adults, and competent adults do not make temporary situations into permanent problems. They pack early. They leave notes on the stove.

But the last Saturday arrived, and he was leaving Sunday, and I was leaving Tuesday, and we both knew that the beach was the one thing we had left that was not on the property, and so we went.

The Subaru belonged to the colony's maintenance man, who had lent it to Toby on the condition that we not, in his words, "go anywhere with it that would embarrass us." We drove east anyway. The check-engine light came on within the first ten minutes, and Toby, who knows more about sensors and their failures than I know about choreography, put his foot on the gas to prove the light was lying. It was not lying. It was merely patient.

We reached the beach in a state of cheerful disaster. The kayak had been borrowed from a volunteer at the marine station down the road, and it was held together with packing tape in the shape of a smiley face, which I found either reassuring or a warning depending on the hour. The wetsuit, also borrowed, was sized for a man a foot taller than Toby and smelled, beneath the algae, of another man entirely. He wore it with the dignity of a man in a borrowed coat.

"Low tide is at one," he said, holding up the tide chart, which he had printed from the official government website and carried in a ziplock bag, because Toby is a man who protects his facts from the weather. "We walk out to the flats at two, turn around at the marker where the mud goes deep, and we're back on the bar by four."

This was the plan. It was a good plan. I have since learned that a plan is a thing you make when you are certain of the tide, the weather, and your own ability to leave.

The walk out was lovely in the way that mud flats are lovely, which is to say it was mostly about not dying. The water had drawn back so far that the ocean looked like it had been moved elsewhere for the afternoon. There was sulfur in the air, and iron, and the strange flat silence of a place that is mostly bottomless. We talked about his research. He talked about wasting disease in sea stars, about how an animal can collapse in a single night, about how he had once spent four days on a beach in Baja cataloguing things no one had asked him to catalogue and had liked it anyway. I told him I had once choreographed a piece about a woman waiting for a phone call that would never come, and that the audience had laughed, which I had taken as a personal failure and which I now take as evidence that I understand people better than I give myself credit for.

We passed the marker. The mud was deep but negotiable. And then we did the thing we did all summer, which was linger.

I don't know what it was about that particular stretch of flats. The light was going sideways and gray. A gull stood on a post like a small, furious accountant. We talked about the residency, about the colony's new director, about whether the farm school's original barns had been built by people who were as badly housed as we were. We talked about nothing. We talked about everything except the thing, and both of us were aware of the thing the way you're aware of a fire alarm that hasn't gone off yet.

At one point he said, "There's a position in Iowa," and stopped, and I watched him look at the mud as if it might have an answer.

"Monday's the deadline to answer," he said.

"Iowa," I said.

"University lab. Permanent. It's, it's the kind of thing you say yes to."

I said, "You're saying yes to it."

"I'm saying it's the kind of thing," he said, and then he said, "I misread the tide."

It came in the way the tide always comes in when you've been standing on a bar too long, which is to say it arrived without announcement, first as a sound, a sucking of water into the channels around us, and then as a line of it moving uphill across the flats like a slow animal. Toby looked at the chart. He looked at the water. He looked at the chart again, and I saw him do the arithmetic, and I saw the arithmetic fail him.

"The channel back floods at three-fifteen," he said.

It was three-fourteen.

We had a minute, then. We took it. He got the kayak, I hauled the sandwiches and the thermos, and we paddled as hard as two people in borrowed equipment can paddle, which is to say with great commitment and limited speed. The water was already at our shins in the shallows, and then at our calves, and then the kayak was half-submerged and useless, and we were on the bar with a kayak strapped to our backs and the sound of the ocean returning like a debt collector.

Here is what I will say in the flat terms of a person who has since written this down twice: it was not terrifying. It was cold, and it was funny in a low way, and it was the first time in six weeks that we had been genuinely, physically, mutually stuck.

The water rose to our knees by four. We stood in the middle of what had been mud flats and was now a shallow lake, and the wind took everything off the clouds at once, and the wetsuit, which had been a joke all afternoon, became the only thing keeping my hands from going numb. Toby held the ziplock bag over his head like a hat.

"You want the coffee?" he asked.

"I want the coffee," I said.

We sat in the kayak, which floated, which was the one thing it was ever going to do for us, and we drank lukewarm coffee while the water closed in on us and the sky went the color of the mud. I have a professional interest in what people do with their bodies when they are uncomfortable, and I will tell you what he did. He sat very straight. He held his hands flat on his knees. He did not look at me, which I took to mean he was thinking about what to say, and I did not look at him either, which meant something I was not prepared to say out loud at that moment.

At five the water was at our waists. He took off the wetsuit, which was a brave and stupid move and which I did not stop him from doing because he was cold and because I wanted to see what he would do without the costume.

"The position in Iowa," he said.

"The position in Iowa," I said.

"The answer's due Monday. And I've been, I've been telling myself it's a good thing, and I'm good at telling myself things. That's the whole job. You stand on a beach for four days looking at dead starfish and you tell yourself things until the things become true."

The water was at his chest now, and he was shivering, and the kayak was rocking gently under us both, which was somehow the most reassuring thing in the world.

"What's the thing you're not telling yourself?" I said.

He looked at me then. The wind was doing something to his hair that made him look younger and more stupid than he was, and I thought about how he had spent six weeks in this country pretending the ocean was only a workplace.

"I want to see you again," he said. "That's the thing. It's not a scientific thing. It doesn't have a deadline, but it has one anyway, because you're leaving Tuesday and I'm leaving Sunday and Iowa is a long way from anywhere you've ever mentioned."

I should tell you that my heart did not hammer. That would be a lie. What happened was that something in my chest arranged itself into a shape I recognized from other temporary rooms, other temporary contracts, other people who had stood in other shallow water and said the true sentence late.

"I have an audition in September," I said. "In Boston."

"Okay," he said.

"I'm saying it because you asked for the thing I'm not telling myself, and the thing is that I've already put Boston in my calendar as a place that isn't just a stop on the way to somewhere else."

He laughed, and the laugh broke open into something that was less a laugh, and the water sloshed against the kayak, and a crab the size of a thumbnail climbed out of the mud around us and looked at both of us with its little dark eyes and then moved on to its own problems.

"The tide turns at six-fifteen," he said. "We're fine. We're actually fine. The bar's still there under the water."

"That's what you told me at three-fourteen," I said.

"That was different. I had a chart."

"Your chart is in a ziplock bag."

"Which is dry," he said, and then he said, "I misread it because I was watching you instead of the water. That's not an excuse. That's a confession."

The water went out the way it had come in, slowly at first and then with a gathering confidence, and by seven we were wading back across flats that had been ocean an hour ago, the kayak on my shoulder, the wetsuit dripping from his hand, the sandwiches ruined and the coffee gone and the sun gone and the gulls gone to roost somewhere with better judgment.

He drove me back in the Subaru with the check-engine light burning steady on the dash like a small, patient star. We did not talk for most of the hour and a half, which was the longest silence we had had all summer and which felt, against all the advice I've ever received, like the opposite of loneliness.

Outside the colony gate he said, "Iowa's a long way from Boston."

"I know," I said.

"You don't have to answer Monday."

"I know," I said again, and I mean it was a little more than that, but the car was stopped and the streetlight above us was flickering and there were two days left in my residency and one left in his and neither of us was going to convert the last hour into a ceremony.

"Next time we do this," he said, "you watch the chart. I'll watch you."

He said it like it was a scheduling note. He said it like it was tide table data, a fact to be filed in the ziplock bag. And I said, "Deal," and got out of the car, and the door shut behind me with the small sound that a door makes when it is closing on a thing that is not yet over.

The light on the Subaru stayed on a moment in the dark after he pulled away, and then it was just a point of red moving east toward a life he had not yet answered yes to, and I went inside to my studio, where my things were already half-packed, and I wrote down, in the notebook I keep for things worth keeping: Boston, September.
